Nurture
NUR-chur
n. (training, discipline, upbringing; the father's charge in Ephesians 6)
From Old French norriture, nourishment, from Latin nutrire, to feed; and so a rearing that both feeds and forms. The Greek word Paul uses is paideia, the whole discipline of a child. It occurs once.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. The verse is addressed to fathers specifically, and it has a negative and a positive half that belong together. Provoke not to wrath — the parallel in Colossians gives the reason, lest they be discouraged. Then the charge: bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord, which is discipline and verbal instruction together, and of the Lord, meaning his and not the father's own. The Old Testament had described the method in detail long before: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. That is not a curriculum but a life lived audibly in front of children. Proverbs gives the promise the whole enterprise leans on: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it. And the paragraph opens with the child's own duty, which the father cannot discharge for him: Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): that which nourishes; food; diet; also education; instruction; the discipline which forms manners and character.

NURTURE, n. That which nourishes; food; diet.

NURTURE, n. Education; instruction; the discipline which forms the manners and character.

ADMONITION, n. Gentle reproof; counseling against a fault; instruction in duties; caution; direction.

PROVOKE, v.t. To call into action; to arouse; to excite; to make angry; to offend.

DISCIPLINE, n. Education; instruction; cultivation and improvement, comprehending instruction in arts, science, correction, and government.

Key Scripture

Eph 6:4 — "And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord."

Eph 6:1 — "Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right."

Deu 6:7 — "And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."

Pro 22:6 — "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it."

Modern Corruption

Parenting is outsourced to school, church programme, or screen, or else reduced to management of behaviour; Scripture charges fathers personally with a formation that is both discipline and instruction, and makes it the Lord's and not the parent's own.

expand to see more

Two failures sit on either side of Ephesians 6:4. The first is harshness, which the verse names directly — provoke not your children to wrath — and Colossians explains, lest they be discouraged. A father can be doctrinally correct and crush a child, and Scripture treats that as disobedience to this command rather than as rigour. The second failure is abdication, handing the formation to institutions and calling it education. Deuteronomy 6 assumes a father talking about the commandments in the house, on the road, at bedtime, and at waking, which no programme can do on his behalf.

The dictionary holds the creational order this verse assumes: the father bears the charge, the mother is honoured with him in the fifth commandment, and children are commanded to obey their parents in the Lord. And the phrase of the Lord keeps the whole thing from becoming a family religion, because the nurture and admonition belong to Christ and not to the man administering them. Proverbs 22:6 is a proverb and not a contract — it states the ordinary way God works and is not a guarantee that binds him — but it is the promise on which generations of faithful fathers have laboured, and it remains true of the way God ordinarily deals with households.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek paideia (G3809), the training and discipline of a child; nouthesia (G3559), admonition, warning instruction; ektrepho (G1625), to rear up to maturity.

expand to see more

Greek paideia (G3809) — the whole training and discipline of a child; rendered nurture.

Greek nouthesia (G3559) — admonition, instruction by word, warning; and admonition of the Lord.

Greek ektrepho (G1625) — to nourish up, to rear to maturity; bring them up.

Greek parorgizo (G3949) — to provoke to anger; provoke not your children to wrath.

Hebrew shanan (H8150) — to whet, to sharpen, to teach diligently; thou shalt teach them diligently.

Usage

"“bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” — the single occurrence."

"“provoke not your children to wrath” — the negative half of the charge."

"“thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” — the method, in Deuteronomy."
